title: Mignonne, allons voir si la rose (first stanza)
author: Pierre de Ronsard
source_notes: Renaissance French original; translation by Andrew Lang, 1888.
reading_notes: Ronsard's famous carpe-diem ode. A young man invites his beloved to look at a rose, which by evening has lost its petals — an emblem of her own vanishing youth. Note Renaissance French spellings: 'qui ce matin avoit desclose' preserves older forms of avait and déclose.

lines.original: Mignonne, allons voir si la rose
lines.english: Sweetheart, let us go see if the rose
lines.gloss: Mignonne = 'sweetheart, little darling' (vocative); allons = 'let us go' (1st plural imperative of aller); voir = 'to see' (infinitive); si = 'whether, if'; la rose = 'the rose' (nominative).
Qui = 'which' (relative); ce matin = 'this morning'; avoit = 'had' (archaic for avait, imperfect of avoir); desclose = 'opened, unfolded' (archaic past participle of déclore; feminine).

lines.original: Sa robe de pourpre au soleil,
lines.english: Her robe of purple to the sun,
lines.gloss: Sa = 'her' (feminine possessive); robe = 'robe, dress'; de pourpre = 'of purple' (genitive of material); au soleil = 'to the sun' (à + le; dative of direction).
A point perdu = 'has not lost' (perfect of perdre with archaic point negation); ceste = 'this' (archaic for cette, feminine); vesprée = 'evening' (archaic for vêprée).

lines.original: Les plis de sa robe pourprée,
lines.english: The folds of her purple gown,
lines.gloss: Les plis = 'the folds' (nominative plural); de sa robe = 'of her gown'; pourprée = 'purple-colored' (feminine adjective agreeing with robe).

lines.original: Et son teint au vostre pareil.
lines.english: And her hue so like thine own.
lines.gloss: Et = 'and'; son teint = 'her hue, complexion'; au vostre pareil = 'equal to yours' (archaic vostre for vôtre; dative + predicate).
